parts.title: A part-time job at a garden centre
parts.context: A student phones a garden centre about a weekend job.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a student phoning a garden centre about a part-time job. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Greenacre Garden Centre, Ruth speaking.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Hello, my name's Ben. I saw your advert for a weekend job, and I'd like to find out more.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Thanks for calling, Ben. The job is in our plants department, looking after the plants and helping customers choose them.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The job is in the plants department, so 'plants' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: How many hours would it be?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: It's eight hours on Saturday and eight on Sunday, so sixteen hours a week.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That's fine. I'm at college during the week. And what's the pay?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: For staff under eighteen it's a bit less, but how old are you?

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Nineteen.

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Then it's thirteen pounds an hour. And all staff get a discount of twenty percent on anything in the shop, which is popular with people who have gardens.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Is there a uniform?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: We give you a green shirt and a fleece. You need to wear strong boots, because you'll be moving heavy pots, and we can't let you work in trainers.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: I've got some. When would the job start?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: We need people from the beginning of May. That's when the summer plants arrive and we get really busy.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: How do I apply?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Just email me. I'm Ruth Mallory, that's M-A-L-L-O-R-Y, and my address is on our website.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Got it. And when are the interviews?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: The advert says Tuesdays, but that's a mistake. The interviews are on Thursday afternoons.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Do I need to bring anything?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Just the names of two referees. A teacher would be fine, or a previous employer.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Is it a normal interview?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Mostly, but there's also a short practical test. We'll ask you to move a plant into a bigger pot, so we can see how carefully you work.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: That sounds fun. And is there any training?

script.speaker: ruth
script.text: Yes. On your first day, everyone does a safety course, mainly about lifting heavy things and using the machines. After that you'll work alongside one of our experienced staff.

script.speaker: ben
script.text: Great. I'll send my email today. Thanks.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A harbour museum and its sailing ship
parts.context: A guide welcomes visitors to a harbour museum with a restored sailing ship.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide welcoming visitors to a harbour museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: Good morning, and welcome to Westport Harbour Museum. My name's Graham. Let me show you around the site using the map in your guide. We're at the entrance, at the bottom of the map, and the visitor centre, on your right, is where you bought your tickets.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: Directly opposite the visitor centre, on the left of the path, is the café. It does a very good fish soup, if you're hungry later.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: As you walk up the main path towards the harbour, about halfway along on your left, you'll pass the boat-building workshop, where our volunteers still build small wooden boats by hand.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: When you reach the quayside, turn left and walk right to the end. The long, narrow building there is the rope-making shed. Ropes had to be made in one piece, so the building is over a hundred metres long.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: If you turn right on the quayside instead, at the far end you'll find the children's play ship, which is very popular with younger visitors.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: And to go on board the Northern Star herself, use the gangway at the edge of the quay, straight ahead of you at the top of the main path.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: A little about the ship. The Northern Star was built in eighteen seventy. She sometimes carried a few passengers, but she was designed to transport coal along the coast, and she did that for almost fifty years.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: The restoration took twelve years. Raising the money was actually the easy part, thanks to a large grant. The real difficulty was finding oak trees big enough to replace the original timbers. Some of the wood came from three different countries.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: When you go on board, do visit the lower deck. That's where the sailors slept, and you're welcome to lie in one of the hammocks to see how uncomfortable it was. The ship's wheel is upstairs, but it's a copy, and please don't try to turn it.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: You can take photographs anywhere on the site and on board, but please don't use a flash inside the ship, because the light damages the old paintwork.

script.speaker: graham
script.text: And you've chosen a good week to visit. Children always get in free, of course, and there's a new exhibition opening next month. But this week, for the first time in a hundred years, our volunteers will raise the sails, at three o'clock every afternoon. It's quite a sight.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A field trip to a wind farm
parts.context: Two environmental science students talk about a field trip to a wind farm.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students, Owen and Lucia, talking about a field trip to a wind farm. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: So, Lucia, what did you think of the wind farm?

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: I'd seen so many photos that I knew the turbines would be huge. And they were much quieter than I expected. But the most interesting part for me was the control room. Just one person was watching all forty turbines on a screen.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: That was impressive. Did you hear what the guide said about the colour?

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: That they're painted that pale grey so they blend in with the sky, and don't stand out so much in the landscape.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Yes. I'd assumed it was so that pilots could see them. Anyway, what was the worst part of the trip, in your opinion?

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: Not the guide, she was excellent, and lunch was fine. It was the coach. Four hours there and back for a two-hour visit.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Agreed. Now, the report. What should we focus on? Most of the other groups are writing about the effect on birds.

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: And we couldn't get any real figures on the cost of the electricity. But we did interview people in the village. Why don't we focus on what local people think?

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Good idea. How should we present their opinions? A pie chart of who's for and against?

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: That loses all the detail. I'd rather use quotations from the interviews, in their own words.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: Fine, quotations it is.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: So, the farmer first. He rents some of his land to the company, and he said the payments are the only reason he can keep the farm going. He also said his sheep don't even notice the turbines.

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: Then the woman who runs the village shop. She said the engineers come in every day, and she's had to take on two extra staff.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: The retired teacher was the most negative. She said the turbines have ruined the view from the hill where she's walked for forty years.

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: And the young mother. She was against the wind farm at first, because she was worried about noise at night. But now she says she hardly notices it, and she's in favour.

script.speaker: owen
script.text: And the man who runs the pub said he doesn't mind wind power at all, but they should have built the turbines out at sea, where nobody would see them.

script.speaker: lucia
script.text: That's a good range of views. Let's start writing.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: earthworms and the soil
parts.context: A biology lecture about earthworms, from Darwin's research to their spread in North America.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about earthworms. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about an animal most people never think about, unless they're gardeners: the earthworm.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: One person who thought about them a great deal was Charles Darwin. His very last book, published in eighteen eighty-one, was entirely about earthworms, and he studied them for more than forty years.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Some of his experiments were rather charming. To find out whether worms could hear, he kept them in pots and played the piano to them. They showed no reaction at all. But when he put the pots on top of the piano itself, they reacted immediately, because they could feel the vibrations.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Darwin also measured how quickly objects lying on the surface of a field were gradually buried, as worms brought fresh soil up from below. He found that stones could disappear under the soil in just a few decades.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So how do worms help the soil? First, you need to know that worms have no lungs. They breathe through their skin, which is why it must always stay moist.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: They feed by pulling dead leaves down into their burrows, which brings organic material deep into the soil. At the same time, their tunnels let air and water into the ground, which helps plant roots to grow.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: And what comes out of the other end, the small piles called casts, is extremely rich in nutrients, far richer than the soil around it.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Worms are very sensitive to vibration, and some birds take advantage of this. Gulls, for example, can be seen tapping their feet on wet grass. It's thought that this copies the vibrations of rain, which makes the worms come up to the surface.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, a surprise. In much of northern North America, earthworms are not native at all. The original worms were wiped out by the ice that covered the region in the last Ice Age. Today's worms arrived with European settlers, in soil and in the roots of plants they brought with them.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In forests, these new worms eat the thick layer of fallen leaves on the ground, which harms wildflowers that depend on it. And they are still spreading, often because people who go fishing throw away their unused bait.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
